lead: A boundary layer begins laminar and turns turbulent past a critical Reynolds number. In the turbulent part the velocity profile is fuller, the layer is thicker, and the wall shear is larger. Even then, a very thin laminar sublayer clings to the wall. It holds only about a fifth of the velocity rise from zero to the free-stream speed U, but there the gradient is steepest and the whole wall shear passes through viscosity. These facts let engineers estimate skin friction on wings, ship hulls, car bodies and long pipes, and explain why a turbulent layer transfers heat better but costs more drag.
prereq: You need 5.1 for growth and the critical Reynolds number, and 5.2 for the profile integrals.

blocks.text: A boundary layer starts at the leading edge with a laminar profile. Fluid moves in smooth layers. At a distance x from the leading edge, the local Reynolds number tells which regime is present.

blocks.where: Re<sub>x</sub> is the local Reynolds number, dimensionless; U is the free-stream velocity in m/s; x is distance from the leading edge in m; ν is kinematic viscosity in m²/s.

blocks.text: Below Re<sub>x</sub> ≈ 5×10⁵ the layer is normally laminar. Above it, small disturbances grow and the layer becomes turbulent. The transition point is x<sub>c</sub> ≈ 5×10⁵ν/U.

The two profiles look different. The laminar profile is rounded: velocity rises slowly from the wall and the layer stays thin. The turbulent profile is fuller. A useful engineering fit for its outer part is the 1/7 power law.

blocks.where: u is velocity at height y above the wall in m/s; U is free-stream velocity in m/s; y is height above the wall in m; δ is boundary layer thickness in m. This law fails very near the wall.
δ<sub>lam</sub> is laminar boundary layer thickness in m; δ<sub>turb</sub> is turbulent boundary layer thickness in m; x is distance from the leading edge in m; Re<sub>x</sub> is Ux/ν, dimensionless.

blocks.text: The turbulent layer is thicker. At the same x and U it grows like Re<sub>x</sub><sup>−1/5</sup>, while the laminar layer grows like Re<sub>x</sub><sup>−1/2</sup>. At x = 2 m with ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s (so Re<sub>x</sub> = 2×10⁶), the laminar estimate is 7.1 mm and the turbulent estimate is 41 mm. A fuller profile carries more momentum close to the wall, so the wall shear and skin friction are higher. This is why a turbulent layer removes heat faster but costs more drag.

sections.h3: The laminar sublayer near the wall

blocks.text: No-slip still holds at a turbulent wall: u = 0 at y = 0. Very close to the wall, turbulent eddies are suppressed by viscosity. This thin sheet is the laminar sublayer. Above it is a buffer layer where neither the viscous law nor the turbulent law fits. Above that is the turbulent core.

blocks.where: y<sup>+</sup> is the dimensionless wall coordinate; y is height above the wall in m; u<sub>*</sub> is friction velocity in m/s; ν is kinematic viscosity in m²/s. The viscous sublayer is often taken below y<sup>+</sup> ≈ 5; the buffer layer lies roughly between 5 and 30.

blocks.text: The friction velocity is a measure of wall shear. For a flat plate it is found from the skin friction coefficient.

blocks.where: u<sub>*</sub> is friction velocity in m/s; U is free-stream velocity in m/s; C<sub>f</sub> is the local skin friction coefficient at the same station, dimensionless; δ<sub>s</sub> is laminar sublayer thickness in m; ν is kinematic viscosity in m²/s.

blocks.text: Textbooks quote the sublayer edge either at y<sup>+</sup> ≈ 5 (purely viscous part) or at y<sup>+</sup> ≈ 11.6, where the linear law meets the logarithmic law of the wall. The common engineering formula δ<sub>s</sub> ≈ 11.6ν/u<sub>*</sub> uses the second convention. With the first convention δ<sub>s</sub> ≈ 5ν/u<sub>*</sub>; for the numbers below that gives 0.11 mm instead of 0.26 mm.

For U = 15 m/s and C<sub>f</sub> = 0.004, u<sub>*</sub> = 0.67 m/s and δ<sub>s</sub> = 0.26 mm. The whole boundary layer at the same condition is about 41 mm, over 150 times thicker. Larger C<sub>f</sub> raises u<sub>*</sub>, raises wall shear τ<sub>w</sub> = ρu<sub>*</sub>², and squeezes the sublayer thinner. The universal velocity profile in wall units and Prandtl's mixing length explain these layers further; only a few universities teach them.

figure.caption: The stack runs from the free stream down to the wall. Notice that the laminar sublayer is a fraction of a millimetre while the whole turbulent layer is tens of millimetres.

spec.aria: The layers stacked from free stream down to the wall, with the thin laminar sublayer highlighted just above the wall.

examples.question: Air with ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s flows at U = 15 m/s over a 2 m long flat plate. Find the transition point, the boundary layer thickness at the trailing edge, and the laminar sublayer thickness there. Use Re<sub>c</sub> = 5×10⁵ and C<sub>f</sub> = 0.072/Re<sub>L</sub><sup>1/5</sup> for the turbulent plate.
steps: Transition point: x<sub>c</sub> = Re<sub>c</sub>ν/U = 5×10⁵ × 1.5×10⁻⁵ / 15 = 0.5 m. The layer is laminar for the first 0.5 m and turbulent after that.
At the trailing edge x = 2 m: Re<sub>x</sub> = Ux/ν = 15 × 2 / 1.5×10⁻⁵ = 2.0×10⁶. Since 2.0×10⁶ > 5×10⁵, the layer is turbulent there.
Turbulent thickness: Re<sub>x</sub><sup>1/5</sup> = (2.0×10⁶)<sup>1/5</sup> = 18.2. δ = 0.37x/Re<sub>x</sub><sup>1/5</sup> = 0.37 × 2 / 18.2 = 0.041 m = 41 mm.
Laminar formula if wrongly used: δ = 5x/√Re<sub>x</sub> = 5 × 2 / √(2.0×10⁶) = 10 / 1414 = 0.0071 m = 7.1 mm. The laminar estimate is about six times too small.

Skin friction: for plate length L = 2 m, Re<sub>L</sub> = 2.0×10⁶, so C<sub>f</sub> = 0.072/Re<sub>L</sub><sup>1/5</sup> = 0.072/18.2 = 0.00396. This C<sub>f</sub> is the mean value for the whole plate; using it as the local value at x = 2 m is an approximation and slightly overstates the local wall shear.
Sublayer thickness (edge at y<sup>+</sup> ≈ 11.6): δ<sub>s</sub> = 11.6ν/u<sub>*</sub> = 11.6 × 1.5×10⁻⁵ / 0.67 = 2.6×10⁻⁴ m = 0.26 mm.
examples.answer: Transition occurs at x = 0.5 m; at the trailing edge Re<sub>x</sub> = 2.0×10⁶, δ = 41 mm, and the laminar sublayer is 0.26 mm thick.
examples.check:
nu = 1.5e-5
U = 15.0
x = 2.0
xc = 5e5 * nu / U
Rex = U * x / nu
delta = 0.37 * x / Rex ** 0.2
delta_lam = 5 * x / Rex ** 0.5
Cf = 0.072 / Rex ** 0.2
ustar = U * (Cf / 2) ** 0.5
sub = 11.6 * nu / ustar
for v in (xc, Rex, delta, delta_lam, Cf, ustar, sub):
    print('{:.7g}'.format(v))

traps: Using the laminar formula after transition: at Re<sub>x</sub> = 2×10⁶ it gives 7.1 mm instead of the turbulent 41 mm.
Confusing the laminar sublayer with the whole boundary layer. The sublayer is about 0.26 mm here; the layer is 41 mm.
Mixing Re<sub>x</sub> with Re<sub>L</sub> in C<sub>f</sub>. Both are dimensionless, but x is the local distance and L is the full plate length.
Using U instead of u<sub>*</sub> in y<sup>+</sup> or in the sublayer formula. u<sub>*</sub> is much smaller, about 0.67 m/s here against 15 m/s.
Putting dynamic viscosity μ in Reynolds number. Re uses kinematic viscosity ν in m²/s; μ has units Pa·s.

quiz.q: State the critical Reynolds number for a flat-plate boundary layer and the two thickness formulas.
quiz.a: Transition is normally near Re<sub>x</sub> = 5×10⁵. Laminar: δ = 5x/√Re<sub>x</sub>. Turbulent: δ = 0.37x/Re<sub>x</sub><sup>1/5</sup>.

quiz.q: Why is a turbulent boundary layer thicker than a laminar one, yet has a fuller velocity profile?
quiz.a: Turbulent mixing carries high-momentum fluid downward and spreads the disturbance faster, so the layer grows thicker. The same mixing fills the outer profile, so u stays closer to U over more of the height; the profile is fuller.

quiz.q: Air with ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s flows at U = 10 m/s over a flat plate. At x = 1.5 m, find Re<sub>x</sub> and the turbulent boundary layer thickness.
quiz.a: Re<sub>x</sub> = Ux/ν = 10 × 1.5 / 1.5×10⁻⁵ = 1.0×10⁶. This is above 5×10⁵, so use the turbulent formula. Re<sub>x</sub><sup>1/5</sup> = 15.85. δ = 0.37 × 1.5 / 15.85 = 0.035 m = 35 mm.

quiz.q: For U = 15 m/s, C<sub>f</sub> = 0.004 and ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s, find u<sub>*</sub> and the laminar sublayer thickness.
At a fixed x, U is doubled. How do Re<sub>x</sub>, turbulent δ and the laminar sublayer change?
quiz.a: Re<sub>x</sub> doubles. δ<sub>turb</sub> varies as Re<sub>x</sub><sup>−1/5</sup>, so it falls to 2<sup>−0.2</sup> = 0.871 of its old value. C<sub>f</sub> falls weakly with Re, so u<sub>*</sub> rises strongly with U. The sublayer varies as ν/u<sub>*</sub>, so it becomes thinner.

quiz.q: Why can the 1/7 power law not be used right at the wall?
quiz.a: At y = 0 the law gives u = 0, but its slope du/dy becomes infinite. An infinite slope would mean infinite wall shear. The real wall region is the viscous sublayer, where the velocity is nearly linear and viscosity controls the shear.

quiz.q: What is the buffer layer, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: The buffer layer lies between the viscous sublayer and the turbulent core, roughly 5 < y<sup>+</sup> < 30, where y<sup>+</sup> = y u<sub>*</sub>/ν and u<sup>+</sup> = u/u<sub>*</sub>. Neither the viscous law (u<sup>+</sup> = y<sup>+</sup>) nor the logarithmic law of the wall fits well there, and it controls much of the transition between wall-dominated and turbulence-dominated behaviour.

beyond: Not for the exam. CFD codes mesh the near-wall region with y<sup>+</sup> values matched to wall functions or resolve the sublayer directly; a poor y<sup>+</sup> choice corrupts drag and heat-transfer predictions. Riblets, polymer additives and suction or blowing are used to delay transition, thin the sublayer and cut fuel burn. Search for 'law of the wall', 'y-plus mesh', 'turbulent boundary layer control' and 'skin friction drag reduction'.
